utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, is there any matters that the parties would like to mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one matter that the Prosecution was kind enough to raise with me. It's been indicated by my learned friend that the witness has some blood pressure and -- and possibly anxiety problems. Can I indicate I have no difficulty with any measure that the Prosecutor wants to take to minimise that stress, and -- if she needs breaks and so on, there won't be any need to ask for my approval about it. We agree that it can be managed however it has to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Morrissey for that. But there is one other matter I will raise. During the -- the testimony of this particular witness, there will be names which might be able to identify her, and that will be the time I would be asking to go into closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see there's no problem for that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no difficulty with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This request is granted. Well, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemnly declare -- solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Can we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you see the solemn declaration on the screen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a technical hitch. Her picture is not being scrambled. She's got protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I was informed that we could see the image in the courtroom but not outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may have been a misunderstanding. I had asked for facial distortion, but now we've already seen her face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's only for the people in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Only for the people in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah, not outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's not outside? Oh, that's all right then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We've already checked -- we've already checked --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The people in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll check it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the -- the situation has now been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you have a sheet of paper in front of you which is called your pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the name written there and the date of birth written there are indeed yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, they are there. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That will be MFI165, Your Honours, and I would like to now tender it under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Morrissey? Thank you very much. It is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell me first what date did you move to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where were you before you moved to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I lived in Capljina. I had an apartment there, but I was born in Grabovica. Also, my husband was born there. It's my home town. So after we retired, we returned to live in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the ethnic composition of Grabovica in 1990, when you were there first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Pure Croat Catholics. It was always like that in that village. There were no other ethnic groups there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: About how many families lived in Grabovica at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: On the left and the right bank in between us is the Neretva River, the main road, the railroad. There were about 160 families, smaller or larger ones, but those were people who had always lived there. There were also some new weekend homes that were being built and so on. So I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, did there ever come a time when this changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well, when there was something which happened in the village which changed this 100 per cent Croat inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Before 1993, there was the war. I don't know -- let's say against the Serbs and -- but we didn't really feel that war so much. There were tensions. That's how it was. The road is there. Cars were passing by. But we didn't really feel much until 1993. In 1993, in May, on the 10th of May, the B and H army came, and then the changes started to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was the first change that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The first change was on the 10th, when the army entered our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this was the ABiH army, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We have a hydroelectric power station. They were guarding it. This was done by the HVO, the Croat army, the police. However, the B and H army came and took everything under control: The village, the people, the power plant. And before that, when it was becoming more dangerous, a lot of young people left with children. Many young people went to Mostar, Herzegovina, to other safer places. Because we're in a valley, and there is nobody who could defend us from anything there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And how many people do you -- would you say remained in that village after the younger people fled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: There were about 100 of us, even more of us from the left -- east side and from the west side. There were a few young people. And that morning, when the army entered, even those few young people who were able to fled to the woods. The youngest person was a girl of four and her father. There were no children at all because their mothers had taken them away and their fathers. It was mostly us, the elderly people, or middle-aged people, let's say, who stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... men and women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. About 50. There was a person called Josip. He was maybe about 45. There was another person, Mladen, about the same age. There was another man of 50 or so. Then I can't remember anymore. But that's -- that's more or less the situation, and then there were lots of other people over 50 and over 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I'm going to show you a picture, and this is MFI165, Your Honours, which is 02992354. And I would like you to look at this picture and tell us, please, where is it that you lived in Grabovica. Would you point out the house, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: It's a very -- not a very good photograph. It's difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, shall we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like you to focus your mind back to the beginning of September. Could you tell what happened in the village at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There were reinforcements in September, and their name was something like Tigers, Wolves, Igman's Wolves. They had all these different names. There were about 30 soldiers who lived in these buildings which I marked, in these offices there belonging to the power plant, below this house that belonged to me, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know any of the soldiers themselves? Did you know anyone? Could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No. These were new soldiers who came from Sarajevo. But before, those who were holding the whole of Grabovica under control were from the nearby villages around Jablanica. They were familiar people. They were holding the checkpoints. They walked around our houses on a daily basis. There were a lot of soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And the most recent ones arrived ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me about these recent soldiers. Did you know any names of these recent soldiers which arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: You mean the most recent ones?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The most recent, yes, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. They all had nicknames, Perla, Derla, Juki, Muki. I didn't know any of the names exactly. I only heard one being called by name -- by the name Beca. He was missing three fingers. But he was in our house so to say, but I don't know any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you know who the leader of these soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This first one was getting some food ready. They didn't have a lot of food. They were mentioning Zuka, and Zuka used to come. Once Zuka's deputy appeared. I saw him on the road. Because, as you can see for yourselves, my house is right next to the road. This person was called -- I can't -- Nijaz or Nijad, and Celo -- once this large car stopped in front and then this was this person. He was called Celo. It was some kind of good car model. And this man was called Celo. Zuka often used to come by though and speak with us civilians. Sefer -- well, I'm not going to go on. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, let's ask -- let me and you about Celo first. How did you know it was Celo that -- when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They mentioned it. They said, "Here's Celo. He's coming," and they greeted him. And this was in front of my house, so -- I was afraid, so I was really watching everything with my eyes very carefully. The others were mentioning that as well. The road is there. Perhaps he was on his way to Mostar on that occasion or -- not Mostar. Perhaps Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where were these soldiers staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Like I indicated on the map, these offices which were like huts where the employees of the Grabovica power plant used to work. That's where they were staying. I can show it to you on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, thank you, Witness. I was referring to these new soldiers which came from Sarajevo. Where were they staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The new soldiers were there. The most recent ones weren't anywhere. They were around -- they were put up around the different houses. These were the most insolent ones who came.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come to the insolent part later, but could you tell us which homes were these soldiers put up in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: You mean these most -- most-recent soldiers or these ones who were called Igman's Wolves? In these offices; whereas, in the houses of Maric Marinko; the others, Maric Pero. Most of them were accommodated on the western side. But they were not there for long. All this took place from the 4th or the 5th until the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, did you hear from your -- the people who housed them how they felt about these most-recent soldiers? I will call these most-recent soldiers the Sarajevo soldiers. Is that okay with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's not okay with the Defence, Your Honour. The evidence might be given that that's where they're from by this witness. And if it is, then terminology can be used. Right at the moment there's no such evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, she's already said it, that the most recent came from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could ask that again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, these most recent ones you said which came, did they come from Sarajevo or some other place, or did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but when I mentioned Sarajevo mostly, they came from up there, from Hadzici or Sarajevo. I know that they came from the northern side, from that part. And the way they talked was not the way our people talked where we lived. These were unknown people. To us they were masked, camouflaged with these red scarves or something. They had all sorts of things they were wearing. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever get to know who their -- their boss was, their leader? You know, all soldiers have a leader.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, we did find out. Right away rumours started that these were Sefer's soldiers, and the first ones who were there before they arrived, Cedo's Wolves, Igman's Wolves and whatever, they also said, "Sefer's coming. Sefer's coming." And on one occasion I was preparing food to welcome this Sefer, and I saw Sefer twice as he passed by in a car, and the last time I saw him was on the 8th of May, when he went to see those soldiers. He got out of the car on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Sefer who, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you know who he was before you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I had heard of him, but I didn't know him before and I wanted to meet him on that occasion. I didn't talk to him. I didn't know him personally, but I saw the way the soldiers greeted him. I heard how they addressed him, and I knew that this was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how did they address him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They raised their hands in greeting. They had a special greeting. Oh, something like "Allahu Akbar" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And in what context -- you'd said you'd known about him. In what context had you known about Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: A lot of soldiers used to come to my house and to the other house as well, because at that time we had electric power. The rest of the village didn't have electricity. So we made coffee in my house, and what food there was was cooked in my house. Nobody had much, but what was there was was shared. The soldiers came to take baths in my bathroom and asked to have their laundry washed. And so I heard what they were saying and I knew quite a lot. When Zuka came to visit them, Zuka talked to me as well. He asked me if I was all right. I said I was. He asked if anyone was mistreating me, and I said no. But I lived in dreadful fear. I alone know how afraid I was and everybody else in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'll go back to my question, Witness, and -- which was: In what context did you know about Halilovic? What was said about him for you to know about him and want to meet him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Want to meet him?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I believe you said that you knew he was there and you wanted to -- to greet him. Or what did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I didn't say I wanted to greet him, but a soldier came from among those first soldiers who were put up in those offices down there, and this soldier brought some liver to me and said, "Fry this by 7.00 p.m. Sefer Halilovic is coming." I didn't fry it right away. It was only 2.00. I wanted it to be fresh. I was going to fry it at 6.00 so that the food would be better. But he arrived at 6.00, and I said it wasn't ready because he arrived earlier. And they said, "He's not coming tonight. He'll come next -- the next evening. Don't fry the liver." And then later on they changed their minds and said, "Oh, fry it. We'll eat it and tomorrow we'll find something else." On the next day, I was in that little house of mine, the first house. A car stopped. A man got out. Two others came out with him, and people greeted him. They addressed him as "Sefer," and he went to see those soldiers. That was on the 5th of September. And they mentioned him a lot throughout those four months. When the army entered Grabovica, his name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when they mentioned him, what did they say about him? Who was he? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They said only nice things about him. They said he was coming and they would talk about what villages they had taken. I once heard them talking that they had received 1.000 marks for capturing two villages. That was what the ordinary soldiers said, the privates. I didn't know their names. I had a large living room, and they would sit there. It was already August when the refugees arrived from Capljina and they consorted with the refugee girls, the Muslim girls, and they talked about all this and I listened to everything they said. I was cooking, laying the table. The soldiers would come and go. They would go to take up their shifts and come back. And I listened to everything they were saying. They spoke well of Sefer. He was their superior. Zuka was their superior. Zuka was a very nice man. He was very friendly. He greeted me in a Muslim way. He didn't say good morning, and I didn't know how to reply to that because it's not my religion, but he was a very polite man, a man who had good manners. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you were talking about these soldiers being put into these homes across the river from you. I was -- I had asked you: Do you know what they felt about these soldiers being put into their homes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just raise a matter there? There are no strict rules against hearsay at this Tribunal, and I acknowledge that. But to ask what these people felt is becoming too speculative. What would be permissible, in the circumstances, is to ask what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, these -- these people whose homes you said the soldiers were accommodated in, did they say anything to you about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I'll tell you. When they came to the west bank of the river, these civilians were not allowed to move around a lot. Marinko Maric, who is a relative of mine, came from the other side. He was barely 50 years old. He was an educated man, an engineer, and he said to me, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: (redacted) He had a big house. He said, "Some soldiers have arrived. They are making our lives miserable. They are shooting, singing, shouting, yelling. I don't know how we're going to survive all this." He came to me because the soldiers on my side of the river, the ones I was cooking for and in contact with, he came to ask whether they could protect them. That was at 4.00 in September. It was on the 8th of September. Marinko's face was black. I said, "I'll try." I addressed Beco. And I said, "Beco, some nasty people have come there to stay with civilians," and he said, "I have nothing to do with that. There's nothing I can do about it." Marinko went home, and at 11.00 in the evening both he and his wife and his father and mother were killed. And to this very day their bones have not been found. They were killed on the meadow near their house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, I will talk about people at another time so -- as to who got killed, if that's all right with you, but for now I would like to take you through the -- what you saw and what you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- heard first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Are you asking me about that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm now going to ask you: Could you tell us what happened? Do you remember the 7th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When those soldiers came to that bank, some of them crossed over to our bank sometimes, and you couldn't know who was who and where they were coming from among the soldiers. As soon as they arrived there, you could hear shooting. I'm not saying they were shooting at people. I don't know what they were shooting at. There were bullets going into the lake. Perhaps they were shooting into the air. There was shouting, yelling, singing. They were very rowdy. And this started on the 7th. On the 8th in the evening, as my house was facing those houses on the other bank, I heard when I lay down in the evening and the refugees were lying down in my house -- there were four families. Some I knew from before. They had worked in the same company as I in Capljina. And I heard women screaming on the other bank. I heard a woman screaming, "My God, what's the matter with you people? What have I done to any of you?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And then I heard another woman's house, but I couldn't tell who the woman was. And I couldn't sleep. I could see that something bad was going to happen. When I got up in the morning, a refugee woman arrived from another part of my house, a Muslim house, and she said, "Did you hear anything last night?" And I said, "Yes." And she said, "I didn't sleep either." And this woman said, "You could hear shooting." And I said, "Yes." That was what I heard that night. And on the following morning, that was the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what happened on the 9th in the morning when you got up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When I got up in the morning, a guard arrived. He kept guard on the bridge that's on the photograph. And he called out to my husband. He called him by name. This was a man from another village, and we knew him, and he called my husband by name and he asked if we were still alive. And he said, "Yes." And we asked him what was the matter, and he said, "Ivan Frano was taken away last night." This was a Muslim. And it seems that they were killed on the bridge. And these people lived in a house just a little higher up than our house across the garden, and we got frightened. And this man said to us, "Don't leave your house." And then he went about his business. And I am grateful to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did some -- thank you, Witness. Did somebody else come to your house that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And then a soldier came to our house at about 9.00. I can't be very precise about the time. We got up. The sun was shining. These women were there with me. And then I went to the new house. I was always going back and forth. We lived in the little house, but -- because there was more room there for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: (redacted). I want to have some coffee." We didn't have any coffee. We roasted wheat, and that's what we made coffee with. I went to the kitchen. I said, "I have a little. We'll share it." I shared out a little of the coffee. I poured some for him and some for myself. He was very young. He stayed outside with those girls and the women in my courtyard. And I said to him, "Here's a little coffee. I haven't got much." There was no sugar at all. He said, "If I manage to get some sugar, Auntie, I'll bring you some," and then he left. I saw that the refugees had suddenly become afraid. A girl called out to me. She asked me to go behind the house, and she said, "He told me that Croats had been killed on the other bank. I'm going to Jablanica" - that's 13 kilometres away from us - "to call people we knew," Ibro and Meho, to see if they can save you and your husband. I couldn't go. It was very far. She said she would go there on foot to call the police. They set out, and a doctor --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but if you will please -- firstly, as you've asked for protective measures, not say your own name. And please be mindful of talking about yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And other names which might identify you. That's why I will ask you about names later, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And secondly, I would like to go back to the soldier. And if you could just answer my questions, it will be faster. It will be -- the Judges will be able to understand you better. Now, let's go back to this soldier, Witness, who came to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: After that, did he say anything else to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Not that soldier, no. He didn't say anything else to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there another soldier --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: But it was another --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. At around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: He came to my house. He looked afraid. He mentioned my name. He called me Auntie. And he said, "I have to kill you." And I said, "My son," and he said, "Why are you a Croat? Go and put on pantaloons if you want me to save you." Then I borrowed some pantaloons. You know what pantaloons are. And I put them on. And my husband hid in the cupboard. A refugee who lived with us hid him in the cupboard.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why did he want you to wear pantaloons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: What I understood him to mean is that if I put on pantaloons, he wouldn't. He left and he didn't harm me in any way. He saw that I was terrified. And then he didn't come back anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which -- women of which ethnicity wear pantaloons, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Muslims. Only one or two elderly women who came from Capljina wore pantaloons, because in Herzegovina, in Capljina, nobody wore pantaloons. It's only in Bosnia that Muslim women wear pantaloons.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, can you tell me what happened to you next.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: After all this you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: These two girls went to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you also tell us the date. Is it the next day or the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, what happened on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: On the 9th -- all of this happened on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Did you stay in your house on the 9th that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Further -- further, the police arrived from Jablanica, and just before dusk they called my husband by name. This man said -- the man who was staying in my house, he said, "He's not here." But when they mentioned his name, this man, he had a white armband. Then he went out of the cupboard, and he said, "Get ready. Somebody will come to pick you up. You're going to Jablanica." I asked this man -- I said there was a woman who had no leg and a man who had no leg and two bedridden old people above my house. I asked him not to leave them behind but to take them too. And that's what happened. There were many, many soldiers around our house. Both those who had arrived 20 days before for whom I had cooked. They were around our houses. They had already brought down the livestock belonging to the people they had first expelled from their houses, my brother, my sister, my cousins. These were all elderly people. (redacted) (redacted) He wanted to be with us. And a soldier came along and said, "No, no. Go away. Go away." And those who had left on foot, two of them had already been killed on the road. And somebody arrived, about 10 -- an FAP truck arrived and they put us onto it. This was at around 5.00. It was beginning to grow dark, and they took us to the camp in Jablanica. There was a woman, 82 years old. She had no children, and a soldier said to me, "Come and call her to come with us." She wouldn't listen to me. I asked her to go, and she said she wouldn't. This woman lived a little way above my house. She said she didn't have any sons who were soldiers, that she had not done anything to anyone, and she wouldn't leave, and I heard then that she also had been killed. Her name was Mara.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Very well. There was an FAP truck standing there. There was no fuel then at that time or cars or anything. This was all open, and the bedridden people were carried on blankets. The car stopped and three of us got out to push it, the three of us who were younger. And next to the road I saw a woman who had been in front of my house an hour and a half before that. I saw her lying in the channel, and she was dead. One side of her head was bloody. She was wearing a sheepskin coat. If I can say her name, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, say her name. Who was it? Just the name you can say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Ilka Miletic. Ilka Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And whether did you say -- could you please tell us the exact location that you saw her. And I'd like you to look at this picture again, please. And if you can identify where you saw her, if it's possible from MFI -- it's an exhibit now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] P165. P165.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could I ask the court deputy to tell me what exhibit number this is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] P165.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit P165.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: P165, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would it be possible, Witness, to say where in that picture you saw Ilka Miletic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Mara Mandic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you have last seen Mara Mandic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Ten minutes before I left for Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Mara Mandic again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, never. When we set out for Jablanica, a soldier told me, the one who was gathering up all the people who were ill, he said, "You tell her to come with us. She won't listen to me." So I ran into her garden and I called out to her, "Mara, we're all going to Jablanica. Come with us." She told me that she didn't want to go, that she didn't give birth to any children, she's not to be blamed or guilty for anything, and she did not want to leave her hearth. So she left -- she was left by herself in the village. And I heard that she was killed within the hour and burned in her house. And this was told by the Muslim person who lived in the house across from her, and his wife was so afraid that she fled to a different place. She was afraid to sleep up there. This is the woman whose husband it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: (redacted) He wanted to stay with us. They also told him, "Go. Go," the soldiers. "You don't have any right to stay." He didn't have a jacket. He was only wearing his shirt. He was cold. He was carrying a small bag with his medicines inside. And maybe some 500 metres further up from Ilka is where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear how he was killed and by whom; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The same soldiers. And it's most likely that they had crossed over via the bridge on the map from that western side and they had followed the civilians who were going to Jablanica along the road, and then first they encountered Ilka. Then they met him and my sister. This sister died, was walking in front of them with her husband, and he called out, "Wait for me," but they had heard that one rifle shot had been fired. Then they had heard another one. And then he fell on the road. And this is something that my sister told me when we came to the camp. That was that same evening of the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: After two days -- after two days, we were in the camp. Two guards came who had been on duty at the dam, our acquaintances from Jablanica, they expressed their condolences to me and they said, "There he is, next to the dam by the road dead. What are we going to do with him?" I asked my husband -- I returned to the camp, and he said, "If they can bury him somewhere so that he doesn't get eaten by livestock." However, he was half burned and like that, so they buried him secretly at night so that the soldiers wouldn't see him. They brought him to our house, to our garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you clarify when you said somebody fell after the two shots. Who fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: My sister who was walking in front of them. She saw it. She wasn't killed. She thought well of saying that her son was in the B and H army. So she came out all right, and her husband too. But when there was a shot, she said there were two soldiers walking and there was one shot and then another shot and then he fell on his back because he was walking along the road. And that's where they found him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this would be Ivan Mandic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And then there were these refugees. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, you can in a minute, but I would like you to answer me whether you've seen Ivan Mandic again. Did you ever see his body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The refugees who were in my house at night, so that nobody would know, they brought him back and they buried him so that nobody would know, under an apple tree near our house. And a Muslim man, our neighbour, came to us in the camp -- to the camp from Capljina, and he said what to do. But we didn't dare do anything because of this Becir, so that he's not blamed for doing anything. And then only 1994, on the 5th of September, he was exhumed. His daughters did that together with IFOR. They came, took him to Split. They called me to go from as well. I saw that shirt, just an end of the shirt. There was some -- a part of his arm, his teeth. I felt faint. I went back. I couldn't look at that anymore. His daughters recognised him. And those medicines, that little bag that he had with him, that was all found on him and it was all buried together with him. So that's what they found with him. He was buried in Mostar, but then later he was transferred to Grabovica to be next to his wife, who had died before the war. All of this is the truth, Your Honours. I know everything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness. What I want to do now is to show you a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could the list of the Grabovica victims please be placed, which is P97.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, can I explain to you what I would like you to do, please. I would like you to look through this list, and we'll take each name at a time. And I would like you to tell the Court, please, in the briefest of terms whether you knew such a person and -- and whatever question -- what the circumstances of your knowledge about them, and whether you have seen them again. It will become clear as we take name by name. Is that all right? Can we go to the first name, Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What's the name, the first name there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Pero Culjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell -- tell me about Pero, when you last saw him and whether you've seen him again since the last time you saw him. Those are the two questions I'd like you to answer, please, in respect of each witness, each one that we -- on the list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Pero Culjak lived on the west side in another village. He's the father-in-law of a person that we know from Grabovica. Fourteen days before that, Pero and his wife were brought in front of our houses in a car and his son -- her son-in-law took them to his place so that they wouldn't be alone. These young people had left, so they didn't want them to be alone. So they lived in Grabovica opposite my house on the western side, him and his wife with their daughter and son-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would the wife be --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I saw him 12 days before that and never again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is the wife the next one on the list, Matija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: She was with him, and she was taken to her daughter, and it all ended in the same way for her as it did for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which way was that? How did it end? What do you mean that it all ended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I mean that five of them were killed over there in one house, and these children who saw them saw them dead. And this son-in-law of theirs, Josip, ended dying in a very cruel way. Five of them were in the house. They were killed in the house, and then later the house was torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you've not seen either Pero or Matija again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I did not see any of those victims from the other side, and I have heard a lot of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when did you hear, Witness, that these people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We heard that they were killed on the 9th when these -- this soldier told these Muslim refugees who had come to my house. But I didn't know everybody by name until we had all come together again in the camp. Then this person came from somewhere and they said this and this. And then this Marinko came, Marinko Dreznjak. And until Goran Zadro came also who saw those victims. Goran and Zoran, that's two brothers. One of them used to come over here, and I don't know the other one. And his parents were killed too.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can we just go down the list. 3 and 4, Cvitan and Jela, do you see them? Number 3 and 4 on the list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Cvitan Lovric and Jela.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And where were they living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They lived in the same place where Pero Culjak and Luca lived, and that's where their lives ended too.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when was the last time you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I saw them 12 days before that because he had brought a cow to our village so -- to breed with a bull, and then they went back to their house, and I had heard from two soldiers that she was in the house and that -- when those two soldiers left the house, the house was burned and nobody ever saw them again. I heard some of this only once I had arrived at the camp on the left side. That's as much as I can say about the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you informed when it was that they were killed? Do you know? Just the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Much later afterwards. It was around the 15th of that same month, in September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. Can we now go to number 5. You've already talked about 5 and 6. You've talked about 7. Can I take you to 8, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Anica Pranjic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you -- do you know this person, Anica Pranjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, Anica Pranjic, she didn't have children. She lived on our eastern side. But this Josip Brekalo who had brought his mother-in-law and father-in-law, he also took her to his house. I had seen her ten days before that, because she's Josip's aunt, and she was in that house together with Josip Brekalo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And let's say that we have finished with Luca and Pero Culjak and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened to Anica Pranjic; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think that she was killed together with these other five people, Culjak Matija and Culjak Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I raise a matter here, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they were living together in one house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated earlier on, I understand there's no objection to hearsay as such in this case. But asking a witness what she knows conceals the level of hearsay that we find ourselves at, and that can be a matter of importance. So that if it's to be indicated whether -- that this witness knows how somebody died, then it ought to be made quite clear - in fairness to the witness as well as to the Defence, frankly - what the basis of her knowledge is. It's a simple question that can be asked. There may be no difficult answer. But it ought to be clarified before the witness says what she knows, where she heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But, on the other hand, the Defence has the full opportunity to ask this question during the cross-examination, which is try to clarify something which is not clear in the direct. But anyway, if possible, Ms. Chana could make sure whether it's direct evidence or the hearsay evidence by asking some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, we were talking about -- Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could I know how long your direct examination will last, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I have ten more names, Your Honour. If the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean -- you mean another five minutes will be okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Well, I'm hoping, yes, five to ten minutes maximum, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, if you know, and who told you what happened to Anica Pranjic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This young man, Goran, said that he had seen her dead in Brekalo's house. They lived all together with them. On the 8th I heard wails from -- wailing from that house. But I didn't see those victims, and then later it turned out that this young boy had seen that, and this Marinko Dreznjak also heard from some soldier that they had been killed in that house. That's about it. Later when we came to the camp, it was the same thing. It was said that all five in the Brekalo house were killed, and those five include Anica Pranjic. There's nothing more that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what I would like you to tell the Court every time I ask you a name is who told you about this. Because I know you did not see it yourself, so you have to tell us every time who is it who told you. Now, in Anica Pranjic's case, who told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This Goran told me that he had seen them, Zadro, and that she was with them. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Can I take you to Franjo Ravlic, number 9 on the list, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell me about this person, please. Do you know her -- or him, rather?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Franjo Ravlic -- Franjo Ravlic, these are all relatives. He came to me at 5.00 in the evening to take some tea. He went home.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What date was this, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: But a woman came, a Muslim woman who lived at his house, and she told me such-and-such a thing, "I am feeling sick. Franjo and Ivan Saric were taken away last night, and it seems very likely that they had been killed up on the bridge." Franjo was found in the water in the lake three months later, and this Ivan, he was never found, and I don't have any more to say about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And Ivan is number 10, right, Ivan Saric on the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, that's the person who was with him. They never found him; whereas, Franjo was found in the lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And do you know who it is who told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: These are my neighbours, so his children told me. I was at the funeral of -- for Franjo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When he was being brought from Mostar to Grabovica, to the cemetery there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. Now I will take you to 13 and 14, Josip and Luca Brekalo. Can you very briefly tell me whether you know them and if you know what happened to them and how you know it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them, husband and wife. They lived on the other side towards my house. He waved to me in the evening of the 8th, called me by name, said, "Ciao," and they were all together, the five of them with this Culjak. Luca is the daughter of Pero Culjak. The daughter of Luca and Pero Culjak is Luca also, and Josip is the son-in-law, and then Anica, this was all in one house.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I told you before that I had heard wailing from that house and they were killed. And a refugee, a Muslim woman told me later, who visited me in the camp, that the house had been burned, and I don't know anything more about that but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this Muslim woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And these children saw these victims. Yes, I do. Edinka.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, I may be appearing like I'm being repetitive, but I just simply want to go down the list for good order. So you don't have to answer at any great length. Can I take you to 15, 16, and 17. These are the Dreznjaks. Can you also now briefly tell me about them and what happened to them and how you know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I knew them. They lived in the direction of my house. Only the River Neretva divided us. We would call out to each other. At 1.00 in front of the house I saw the daughter of this person and his wife, but later I heard that they had been killed. And that's how it is. The daughter was found, but the two old people were not found. She was exhumed. Dragica was the daughter. Mara was the mother. Andrija Dreznjak, that was Mara's husband. And there's nothing more I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who told you about this? Could you just tell us this, please, about the Dreznjaks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When we got there to the camp, we learned that right away. There were Muslims there, our neighbours who gave evidence, they were horrified and they regretted what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can I now take you to number 31 and 32 on the list, which is Zivko and Ljuba Dreznjak. Could you tell us about them with the same fashion, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They were killed in front of their house, and there was some manure in front of the house and they covered them up a bit with the manure. He was mentally ill. He had a beard down to his waist. His wife was there as well. His son was driven away, and he heard the shots. And they were found there and buried. I can't remember how much time had gone by. About a year, I think. Their son --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And -- who told you about the fact they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Their son told me, and I went to the funeral. They were my closest neighbours. I can't say anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the last -- there's just one last -- there's number 33. I think this particular one, Witness, you told the -- the lawyer during proofing who's with you that he had in fact died in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have already indicated this to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. It has nothing to do with the events of this month.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And just the last question, now, Witness: All these people that we have talked about from this list, did they all -- could you tell us which period they died in, the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: All of the people we have just talked about except for Jela Lovric and Cvitan - they were killed a bit later - but all the others in August and September, with the exception of Jozo Istuk. It was all in those two days and two nights; that is, there was a night and a day and another day, all these others. I'm sure of that. I know them all. Half of them were related to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I want to thank you very much, Witness. I'm not going to question you any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And thank you very much. Your Honour, we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's high time for us to take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 11.00, about a 30 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm just waiting for an image to appear on the screen and then I'll commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness just excuse me whilst we get a -- an image on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's on my screen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, it now -- I now have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Morrissey, and I am the counsel appearing for Mr. Halilovic, and I have some questions for you firstly about the state of affairs in the village in the time before the soldiers from the north came to that village. Okay? Now, you've indicated that after the time that the Bosnian army took over the village, there were soldiers present on a daily basis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Not a lot. There were soldiers at checkpoints, standing guard on the bridge, on the dam, and also they would pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And those soldiers, as you understood it, had as a commander a man known as Zuka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And as far as you could see, this commander called Zuka made efforts to cause good relations between his soldiers and the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. He didn't do anything special. Zuka would leave and the soldiers, like any soldiers, would go through the houses, would take what they wanted, food, clothing. That's what war is like. It wasn't brilliant, but you could live. We didn't move around much. We didn't leave the yard of our house, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And you were put in the difficult position of having to find a way of living with the young men who were the soldiers in Zuka's army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. But they didn't sleep in our house. They were billeted in some offices belonging to the hydroelectric power plant. That's where they stayed. That's where they lived. And then Jablanica and Grabovica were 12 kilometres apart, and soldiers would often come by car. They would change shifts, and that's what it -- what happened. They would come to the houses to ask us to do things for them. Not everybody in the village. I was especially exposed because my house was close to the hydroelectric power plant and that's why we had electricity, so that I could cook, I could bake things, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And is it the fact that Zuka made available to you medical services and a doctor who came once a week to the hydroelectric plant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, he came. I even knew what his name was. He would come to the hydroelectric power plant every week, to the offices there, and we could go and have a checkup, have our blood pressure measured. And I would see Zuka. We didn't have any transportation to Jablanica. He said he would arrange a bus, but nothing happened. There was no bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just a very quick side question: Did you know people who lived up in the village of Diva Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who -- do you remember the names of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I remember Sevko Sejic. He was a local villager. And then a brother-in-law of his came. I don't know what his name was. They lived there and they had livestock. Sevko Sajic was a forester. There were two families living there. It wasn't far from us. Previously it was a purely Muslim hamlet. But 20 or 30 years ago they all left. They would only come from time to time to work on the land. But Sevko lived there. What do I know? He would visit our village as well, and Sevko wasn't an acquaintance of ours. He acted as if -- I mean, Sevko stopped acting as if he knew us. He began acting as if he didn't know us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Did you go up to Diva Grabovica in this -- in the months of July, August, or September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I didn't go far from my house from May to September. I didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Now, I have some questions about the soldiers who came to the village in the days and weeks before the killings that happened. Did -- I think you've indicated this, but I'll ask you to be clear: Did a group called Cedo's Wolves come to stay in the village about 20 days or so before the incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. And you've already told us this, that those soldiers, Cedo's Wolves, indicated to you that they knew the name Sefer Halilovic and, I think you said, they quite liked him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, some of them at one stage told you that Sefer was coming; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, on the 5th of September, did another group of soldiers called the Handzar Division arrive in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did they have a leader called Dziki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: There were so many nicknames. But as this was on the west bank and I was on the east bank of the river, I couldn't tell you what their names were. They all had nicknames, Riki, Briki [phoen]. I can't even recall them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Nobody had a real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In any event, you've indicated here in this Tribunal that on the 5th the soldiers from Cedo's Wolves provided you with some liver to cook, and you've indicated what you did in relation to that liver. Now, could I just ask you some questions about that, please. First of all, do you clearly recall that it was liver that was provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've given us some detail about the delay before you cooked that liver. So I take it you've got a clear memory that it was liver; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you've indicated too that there were -- there was a false start in the sense that the -- the soldiers told you Sefer was coming, then they told you he wasn't coming, and then ultimately something happened at 6.00; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: What happened was that he didn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have spoken to a Prosecutor in Sarajevo yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And that was a man named Manoj Sachdeva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And when you spoke to him, you knew it was very important to tell the truth to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: He told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And you made every effort to tell him the truth and you did tell him the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to read to you what we've been provided with from the Prosecutor as to that, and I quote this, and you were speaking about Sefer Halilovic here, and this is the quote: "The last time I saw him prior to the massacre was on the 5th of September, 1993 in the afternoon. I was peeking outside my window at my house when I saw some soldiers in a jeep arriving. Sefer Halilovic got down from the jeep and the car went on. And the jeep seemed to be very old." Now, that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: It was dirty, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. That's okay. But the facts that I've read out to you that you told the Prosecutor are true; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, can I go on to another topic, please, and that is the 7th -- I want to move now forward to the 7th of -- of September. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, on the 7th of September -- and I just want to be clear so that you -- so that you're not confused by my questions and so that we're speaking the same language effectively. What you say is that the -- the violence and killings commenced on the 8th and continued into the 9th of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm speaking to you about the 7th, so you understand that's the day before the trouble happened. Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- looking out from your window in your house on the left bank of the Neretva, did you notice three buses led by a jeep driving into the village on the right bank, on the other bank from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I didn't observe the buses because for the most part these soldiers arrived in the evening. I didn't always dare look out, but I did see a jeep on that side and I saw that large numbers of soldiers were around. I didn't see the buses. Whether they stopped above the bridge, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: (redacted), Your Honour. The basis of the objection is that it's misleading the witness and to the extent that she is told there's evidence from him and there isn't. And it's a statement and it's not evidence in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that the word "evidence" means that the evidence has already been admitted into the evidence in this courtroom. "Evidence" here in this connection is just some information, so far as I know. Maybe Mr. Morrissey could make it want more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Witness, I just want to make a submission to the Judge. Would you excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we have to go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please excuse that division, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I won't trouble you with the statement of another witness. What you say is you did not see those buses and that's -- and you never did. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Can I clarify this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I'm actually withdrawing the question, and I'll ask you another question about it and we'll see where we go from there. Okay? Now, the next question is -- about this that regardless of what happened on the 7th, on the 8th you became aware of the arrival of yet another group of new soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it was at this time that shooting, celebrations, and general bad behaviour could be heard by you from your house, even though they were over on the other bank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated earlier on that you were sometimes worried to look out of your window. Is that because you didn't want to be seen to be curious or to be paying too much attention to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. But the house of that witness is on that side, on the east bank, and he could see the buses because they were passing in front of his house, and it's possible that I didn't see any because I didn't dare look always.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, and thank you for that clarification. Now, the way into the village on the -- on the west bank takes a person -- a person coming from Jablanica into that village has to cross over the two bridges, including the iron bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No. If he's going along the main road, then he would cross over to the other side. But if he's taking the train, then that is on the west bank. But the train -- trains weren't operating at that time anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you. I'll -- I'm actually talking about people in cars, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. A person coming down from Jablanica and wanting to go to the right bank, or the other bank from yours, would turn off the road before getting to your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. So that troops going over to the right bank wouldn't necessarily have to drive past your house at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But nevertheless, if you happened to be looking, you might be able to see some of their movements over on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. It's close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Only the road separates us from the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, I'm going to come to the events that happened in a moment. I just want to ask you some questions about the refugees and your dealings with them before I come to those sad events. Okay? Now, the first question is: Is it the fact that at the end of August a large number of refugees of a Muslim background began to appear from HVO-held territory in the Jablanica and Grabovica area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did many of those refugees pass up the road from Dreznica and Mostar on their way to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Came in cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They would come in cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were they sometimes brought up by United Nations officials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you come to know that these were refugees from the area of Capljina and also from Stolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. But I can't say about them all, because I -- I knew practically all of those who came from Capljina. We were colleagues, friends, and I offered them hospitality as much as I could and they lived in the house with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I was going to come to the kindness that you showed to these people, and it might be appropriate to do so in just a moment. But I want to ask you a couple of other questions first. Did you become aware on the night of the 8th, that is, the night when the shooting was going on, that a number of refugees from the Dretelj camp passed through or came to the village of Grabovica and in particular your side of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Did you come to hear that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Perhaps they did, but there were a few who came there. I don't know about -- anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the refugees from the Dretelj camp; let me ask you some questions about that. First of all, your house was already full up, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In fact, you were looking after numerous families.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Because I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Is the -- is the position this: That you heard of the arrival of some of the Dretelj camp people but you didn't see them on the night of the 8th? Is that the correct position or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. But you were told that they were in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. But only three or four people whom I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. Can you recall the names of the three or four that you knew personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I will tell you only one. He was killed by a shell when he came back home. Hajder Dedic. Because he was in my house. I knew him from before, and I allowed him to change his clothes. I can't remember any of the others. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Could I just ask you this: If you were concerned to reveal the identity of any such people, the Court can accommodate that by entering into a private session. So would you please indicate, are there people that -- other people whose names that you remember but who you would prefer not to mention for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I can't really recall the names. I've forgotten the names. There were some younger people there too, and I really cannot tell you anything right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. At what time of the night was it -- I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Because the women which ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The women refugees were not at the camp. They came from homes and houses and apartments. They didn't tell me anything. We lived together, but we didn't spend so much time together because this unfortunate 8th and 9th came very quickly. I cooked. What I had, I gave from the house, from the garden. We were trying to get by as best we could. I can't really say anything else. And perhaps it was them -- or thanks to them that my life was spared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, could I just ask you this: You mentioned one name of a person killed. That was Mr. Dedic. What time of night did Mr. Dedic arrive when you allowed him to change his clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the morning, around 9.00. He was up there in the huts. These were the workers' huts. They were empty, so he spent the night up there. Then he asked about our house, and he came to us and then he changed his clothes at our house. Later he would come to visit me as well, but all of that was very short and it happened within a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And is he -- did you receive a number of visits from people when you were already removed up to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They didn't visit me then, because this all happened within a day. Nobody knew where we would go on the 9th. But before that, women would come to visit me, acquaintances, women that I worked with. Of course they came to visit. And there were also men that I worked with in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let me just ask a question about that: Of the refugees who were in or passing through Grabovica on the night of the 8th and perhaps also the morning of the 9th, were some of those people men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Before the 8th and 9th, there weren't many of them who came. They came about eight or nine days before that, around the 1st or the 28th. It depended. They arrived gradually. They were supposed to be situated in the employee huts which were empty, but that was not possible. So the abandoned houses which had been left by their residents were used to accommodate those people and then also we took them into our houses too. That was my case. For example, the people that I knew from before, I put them up at my house, the wives of the men who had taught my kids at school, I put them all up at my house. We did the best we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, as to the ones who came through on the night of the 8th and the morning of the 9th, do you personally know whereabouts it was that they stopped in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the refugees or the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pardon me. I am thinking of the refugees, with particular reference to the night of the 8th and the 9th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No refugees came to Grabovica on the 8th and 9th. Perhaps they passed by in trucks to go to Jablanica or Prenj or some other places. But in Grabovica all the houses were already filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you know whether -- obviously there was no point anyone knocking on your door because your house was full. Do you know whether those people who passed through that night knocked on any other doors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as my house is concerned, those who were there, they told the others, "There's nothing for you here. You have to find something else for yourselves." So the families who arrived first would tell these others to do that. But on the 8th and 9th, there were no refugees. All of them had already left a few days before. I really don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you recall what time it was you went to bed that night, the night of the 8th, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: On the 8th, I went to sleep at 10.00. I went to bed at 10.00, but I didn't actually sleep at all, because there were three or four houses -- soldiers in my house that night, as well as all these others, and I was making dinner for them. I have a large living area. I was in the new house at the time and I was making dinner, and it all turned out badly. There were three soldiers there that I had never seen before. I said, "Good evening," and he said, "Mehraba," and I didn't know that word, so I didn't greet them and I didn't like that. I didn't think that was very nice. And I also saw some soldiers around my house. There was another house with two doors close to my house.
